snippets.snippet_text: Isaiah 40 opens the 'Book of Consolation'—a dramatic shift from 39 chapters of judgment to divine comfort. But comfort here isn't sentimental; the Hebrew word nachamú (נַחֲמוּ) means both consolation and repentance, implying that God restores not just feelings but the covenant dignity of His exiled people.

When Isaiah commands 'speak to the heart' of Jerusalem (Isaiah 40:2), he's using an idiom that reaches far deeper than comfort—it means to persuade tenderly, to reach the inner core of a broken person. God doesn't merely console; He restores dignity through intimate, personal address.

All four Gospels identify Isaiah 40:3 as John the Baptist's mission, but the verse's original context is even more radical: it promises that every topographical obstacle to encountering God will be removed—valleys lifted up, mountains brought low—making the path to the divine accessible to all.

Isaiah 40:31's beloved promise to 'mount up with wings as eagles' echoes Exodus 19:4, where God told Israel at Sinai: 'I bare you on eagles' wings.' But here, the covenant promise is extended beyond national deliverance to every individual who waits upon the Lord—a radical democratization of divine protection.

In Isaiah 40:26, God claims to 'call them all by their names'—naming every star individually. This wasn't just ancient poetics; it was a covenant claim: if God knows the names of countless stars, He surely knows and calls His covenant people by name. Latter-day Saints recognize this in temple covenants made individually with God.

Isaiah 42:7 defines the Servant's mission—opening blind eyes, releasing prisoners from darkness—language Jesus Himself claimed at His ministry's beginning (Luke 4:18). But notice: liberation isn't metaphorical only; it addresses concrete, embodied suffering, making discipleship inseparable from justice.
